story: Predicting 'am'/'pm' or the next digit inside opening-hours and price strings such as 'h10am-5pm' in listing metadata.
notes: Story genuinely names the category (am/pm or digits inside time/price strings) and every rule token belongs to it; the digit subsets are capacity-limited samples of the digit class, not smuggled-in unrelated tokens. False positives are the same time-string boundary cases (e.g. 'h10am-5[->pm]' contexts the circuit does not own), which is honest.

story: Predicting the comma that follows a day-range abbreviation like 'Mon-Sat' or 'Mon-Fri' in opening-hours strings.
notes: The certified rule sneaks 'pm' into prev_in, so it also fires on commas after time spans ('h10am-6pm[->,]') -- a different pattern the story never claims (several false positives are exactly this). Fix: drop 'pm' from prev_in; the day-name-only rule is what the story actually describes.

story: Inside guidebook listing lines, predicting the space token that follows a semicolon field separator.
notes: The rule (space after any semicolon) is clean, but the certified story overclaims two ways: it says the semicolon 'ends the hours field' (the rule fires after semicolons ending any field -- prices, addresses, wifi icons, as the false positives show) and it appends an unoperationalized 'occasionally re-predicts a landmark noun' clause that no rule field tests. Fixed story matches what is measured; rule unchanged.

story: Inside a listing's info line, predicting the icon-letter tokens that open each field: ' h' for hours, ' t' for tube station, ' G' for 'GOOGLE MAP', ' www' for the website.
notes: The four tokens are exactly the field-prefix category the story names, and in this corpus they occur essentially only in listing info lines, so the target-only rule is a fair operationalization. False positives are other listings' field prefixes the circuit does not own -- honest boundary cases.

story: Via induction on times seen earlier in the passage, completing time-of-day expressions in opening-hours listings with 'pm', 'am', or the '30' of a half-hour.
notes: ' century' (fired after '15th'/'16th' etc.) is an unrelated pattern bolted onto a time-completion story purely to lift the numbers; the story does not name centuries as part of the category. The story also claims 'after a digit' but the rule has no prev constraint. Fix: drop ' century'. A prev_in digit list would tighten it further but would also drop legitimate '.30' cases, so target trim plus is_induction is the minimal honest rule.

story: Predicting the newline that ends a guidebook listing line right after its closing parenthesis (opening hours, tube station, etc.), late in the window where many such lines have already occurred.
notes: Newline-after-')' is a real named category and the position clause is stated in the story, not hidden. It is the late-window twin of circuit 59; low precision (0.23) shows the circuit is weak, but the explanation is not hollow -- false positives are the same listing-terminator contexts owned by circuit 59 instead.

story: Predicting the decimal point after a number -- in clock times ('5.30pm'), prices ('£16.25/9.10'), and other figures throughout listing text.
notes: The certified story claims the period is 'inside a clock time... in opening-hours listings', but the rule is simply 'period after any digit' and demonstrably fires on price decimals, measurements ('1.63m'), and URLs ('www.number10[->.]') -- and the circuit's own positives include those non-time cases, so the circuit itself is the broader pattern. Fix the story to the honest broader category; rule unchanged. (Restricting to clock times via prev2_in ['-'] would also cut real members like 'h10.30am-12[->.]'.)

story: Predicting the newline that closes a listing's parenthesized info line (hours, prices, tube stop) right after the closing parenthesis, relatively early in the window.
notes: Same real category as circuit 40 with the complementary position band, stated openly in the story. Precision 0.667 and false positives that are identical listing-terminator contexts owned by the sibling circuit make this a faithful explanation.

story: Completing weekday ranges in opening hours, above all predicting 'Fri' after the hyphen in 'Mon-Fri'.
notes: The story explicitly narrows itself to the 'Fri'-after-hyphen core and the rule tests exactly that. Precision 0.833; the two false positives ('Sun-Fri', another 'Mon-Fri') are textbook honest boundary cases.

story: Advancing the boilerplate skeleton of a listing's details line: the '(' that opens the phone/map/website block after the name-plus-category header, the ';' that follows a closing parenthesis, and the 'www' that starts the website field after a semicolon.
notes: The certified story claims only 'predicting the opening (' but two of the three targets (' ;' after ' )', ' www' after ';') are mid-line separator continuations, and roughly half the positives and all false positives are those cases -- the rule tests a wider pattern than the story admits. The wider pattern is itself coherent (listing-line boilerplate), so fix the story; rule unchanged.

story: Predicting the day-of-week name at the end of an opening-hours clause, e.g. 'to 10.30pm Sun' or '8am-9pm Sat'.
notes: ' Nov' is a month, not a day of week -- an off-category token slipped into a day-name list to catch 'Apr-Oct/Nov-Feb' season strings and pad recall; the story does not name months. Fix: drop ' Nov'. The remaining rule is a faithful operationalization and the false positives ('Thu & [->Fri]', 'Sat & [->Sun]') are honest boundary cases.

story: Predicting 'am'/'pm' right after the hour digit in opening-times strings.
notes: The certified rule welds two unrelated patterns together -- am/pm after digits AND 'co' after '.' in URLs -- and the story's parenthetical mention of the 'co' half is a readback of the rule, not a genuine single category (the cross-product also licenses nonsense combos like 'am' after '.'). With precision already at 0.158 the padding is doing certification work. Fix: strip 'co' and '.' to leave the real time-completion core. If the URL behavior is real it belongs to a separate circuit (compare 112).

story: Via induction, continuing URL and web-address boilerplate seen earlier in the passage: the dot after 'www', 'co'/'uk' around the dots of '.co.uk', and 'LE' after 'GOOG'.
notes: The certified rule is a grab-bag: targets '-', '\n', ' of' appear nowhere in the story's named category (URL boilerplate), while the story's own 'uk after .co' example is not even in target_in. The AND-of-lists cross-product then licenses pairs like '\n' after 'uk' or ' of' after 'am' that have nothing to do with URLs -- most false positives are paragraph-final newlines. Fixed rule keeps only the URL-continuation tokens the story genuinely names.

story: Predicting the determiner 'the' or 'a' immediately after a linking verb or possessive ('is', 'was', 'are', 'has', ''s').
notes: The certified rule cross-products six function words with seven preceding words, several of which fit neither half of the story's category (' and', ' in' are not determiners; ' including', ' for' are not linking verbs or possessives) -- an arbitrary token grid dressed up as 'function words after linking verbs', at 0.155 precision. The circuit's positives also contain many non-function-word predictions, so even the trimmed core may be optimistic, but determiner-after-copula is the one real sub-pattern visible in the members; the fixed rule keeps exactly that.
